# Korenizatsiya Policy in the Soviet Republics of the South Caucasus in the 1920s–1930s

Korenizatsiya (; indigenization, or "nativization") was a  of the 1920s and early 1930s aimed at promoting local (titular) nationalities in the party and state apparatus, education, culture, and the press. It was intended to strengthen the loyalty of non-Russian peoples to Soviet power, overcome the legacy of Russian domination in the Tsarist empire, and create national elites loyal to Bolshevism.
Background
After the establishment of Soviet power in Transcaucasia (Azerbaijan in 1920, Armenia in 1920, Georgia in 1921), the three republics were united in 1922 into the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic (TSFSR), which existed until 1936. Korenizatsiya in the region was implemented within the framework of the general policy adopted at the 12th Congress of the RKP(b) in 1923, but taking into account the complex ethnic mosaic of the area: Georgians, Azerbaijanis, Armenians, Abkhazians, Ossetians, Adjarians, Kurds, and others.
The policy included transferring office work to local languages, training national cadres, creating national schools and press, increasing the share of titular peoples in party and soviet organs. Together with the New Economic Policy (NEP), korenizatsiya helped stabilize power in a region where nationalist movements had previously been strong.
Georgian SSR
In the Georgian SSR, korenizatsiya was pursued particularly actively and led to a significant increase in Georgian representation in the apparatus. While Georgians dominated leadership in the 1920s, the policy favoured them at the expense of minorities (Abkhazians, Ossetians, Adjarians, Mingrelians). This caused tensions: for example, the "Mingrelian question" in the late 1920s and early 1930s, when Mingrelians were accused of separatism, even though korenizatsiya formally supported the Georgian language and culture. The retreat from strict korenizatsiya in the late 1930s led to a decline in the proportion of Georgians in the republic's population (from 67.1% in 1926 to 61.4% in 1939).
Armenian and Azerbaijani SSR
In the Azerbaijani SSR, korenizatsiya promoted Azerbaijanis (Turkic-speaking population) into leadership positions, although strong Russian and Armenian influence remained in Baku. In the Armenian SSR, the policy strengthened the position of Armenians, especially after the repression of Dashnaks. In both republics, national schools, theatres, and press were created, but interethnic conflicts (especially Armenian-Azerbaijani) limited its effectiveness.
End of the Policy
By the mid-1930s, korenizatsiya was rolled back: repressions began against "bourgeois nationalists,"  the use of Russian increased, and many national cadres were repressed. In 1936, the TSFSR was dissolved and the republics became separate union republics. The policy, originally intended to strengthen the Union, ultimately revealed its limits: excessive emphasis on the national provoked tensions between titular peoples and minorities.
